relationship: Thirst and longing for God
rationale: The deer longing for water expresses the soul's longing for God. Psalm 62 likewise describes the soul thirsting for God and the flesh longing for Him in a waterless land. Both express desire for God through longing for water, without saying the deer was denied access to the springs.

relationship: Longing to approach the living God
rationale: The soul thirsts for the living God and asks when it will appear before His face. Psalm 83 joins longing for the Lord's courts with heart and flesh exulting in the living God, connecting desire for divine presence with that particular designation.

relationship: Tears as food
rationale: The speaker's tears became bread by day and night. Psalm 79 asks whether God will feed the people bread of tears and give them tears to drink; both make prolonged grief into the sufferer's food.

relationship: The taunt asking where God is
rationale: Daily tears accompany the taunt, 'Where is your God?' Joel's priests plead that God's inheritance not become a reproach so that the nations do not ask, 'Where is their God?' The similar taunt occurs in personal lament and communal intercession respectively.

relationship: Approaching God with exultation and thanksgiving
rationale: The speaker remembers and pours out his soul, then says he will pass through the place of a wonderful tent to God's house with exultation and thanksgiving. Psalm 94 invites people to exult and come before God with thanksgiving; the shared approach to God has those two expressions of praise.

relationship: A repeated address to the troubled soul
rationale: Both verses ask why the soul is deeply grieved and disturbing the speaker, tell it to hope in God, and anticipate thanksgiving to the God who is the salvation of his face. This sustained refrain connects the neighboring laments.

relationship: Divine billows and waves passing over the speaker
rationale: The psalm's water imagery culminates in all God's billows and waves passing over the speaker. Jonah uses that same extended statement while praying from the sea creature; the verbal correspondence does not identify the psalm's speaker with Jonah.

relationship: Mercy and song across day and night
rationale: The psalm anticipates the Lord commanding mercy by day and has a song and prayer at night. Psalm 91 commends music to God with declaration of mercy in the morning and truth by night. The daily rhythm joins mercy and worship, with different actions assigned to God and the worshippers.

relationship: Questioning rejection under enemy oppression
rationale: Psalm 41 asks God why He has forgotten the speaker and why the speaker goes downcast while an enemy oppresses. Psalm 42 repeats the downcast and enemy question after asking why God has thrust him away; the opening descriptions of God's apparent withdrawal differ.

relationship: The reproach asking where God is
rationale: The enemies reproach the speaker with 'Where is your God?' Psalm 113 asks that the nations not say 'Where is their God?' Both make denial of God's apparent presence a hostile challenge, without identifying the enemies as the same group.

relationship: same-chapter refrain of hope
rationale: The closing verse repeats the earlier address to the deeply grieved soul, the command to hope in God, and the anticipated thanksgiving. Its recurrence gives the renewed lament the same response of hope that ended the earlier movement.

relationship: Appeal for God to judge a case against wrongdoers
rationale: Psalm 42 asks God to judge the speaker's case against an unholy nation and rescue him from an unjust, deceitful person. Psalm 34 opens by asking the Lord to judge those who wrong the speaker; both seek divine adjudication against hostile wrongdoers, with Psalm 34 also using warfare language.

relationship: The repeated downcast question
rationale: Both speakers question God's apparent withdrawal and ask why they go downcast while an enemy oppresses. Psalm 42 says God thrust him away, whereas Psalm 41 asks why God forgot him; the repeated question preserves that difference.

relationship: Divine truth as guidance
rationale: Psalm 42 asks God to send His light and truth, then says they guided and brought him to His holy mountain and dwellings. Psalm 24 asks God to guide the speaker into His truth and teach His paths. Both connect truth with divine guidance, without changing Psalm 42's completed guidance into a wholly future action.

relationship: Altar approach joined to praise
rationale: Psalm 42 anticipates going to God's altar and giving thanks with a lyre. Psalm 25 anticipates going around God's altar to hear praise and recount His wonders. Both place praise at an approach to the altar, while describing different movements and sounds.

relationship: The refrain shared by adjacent laments
rationale: Psalm 42 ends with the same questions to the deeply grieved soul, command to hope in God, and anticipated thanksgiving found in Psalm 41. The repeated wording makes a concrete literary connection between the neighboring poems.

relationship: Fathers transmitting God's ancient works
rationale: The community says its fathers announced the work God did in ancient days. Psalm 77 likewise speaks of what the fathers recounted and of announcing the Lord's mighty acts and wonders to another generation; both explicitly transmit divine deeds through generations.

relationship: God planting His people
rationale: Psalm 43 contrasts God's destruction of nations with His planting of the fathers. The sea song asks God to bring and plant His people in the mountain of His inheritance. The planting image describes divine establishment of the people, expressed as remembered action and petition respectively.

relationship: Possession of the land beyond human weapons
rationale: The psalm denies that the fathers inherited the land by their sword or were saved by their arm, crediting God's power and favor. Joshua's retrospect likewise denies conquest by their sword or bow and describes land and cities given without their labor.

relationship: God as King who brings salvation
rationale: Psalm 43 calls God its King and describes Him as the one who commands Jacob's salvations. Psalm 73 calls God the community's King and says He worked salvation in the earth. Both pair divine kingship with salvation, using a present description and remembered action respectively.

relationship: Goring peoples as an image of victory
rationale: The community says it will gore enemies through God. Joseph's blessing depicts horns with which he will gore nations and identifies Ephraim and Manasseh. Both use the animal action for human victory, but the psalm does not name Joseph or those tribes.

relationship: Salvation not secured by weapons
rationale: The psalmist refuses to hope in his bow or expect salvation from his sword. David announces that the Lord does not save by sword and spear because the battle belongs to Him. Both explicitly deny that military weapons are the source of salvation.

relationship: Rejection and God's absence from the forces
rationale: Both verses say God rejected the people and will not go out with their forces. Psalm 43 adds their shame; Psalm 59 introduces the statement with a question. The extended wording, including the army's lost divine accompaniment, is shared.

relationship: Defeat before enemies under divine action
rationale: The psalm attributes the people's retreat before enemies to God. Leviticus threatens falling before enemies and flight when God sets His face against the disobedient. The military reversal is comparable, but Psalm 43:18 denies covenant unfaithfulness, so Leviticus's stated cause is not imposed on the lament.

relationship: Scattering among the nations
rationale: Psalm 43 says God gave the people like sheep for eating and scattered them among nations. Leviticus threatens scattering among the nations in its covenant sanctions. The scattering language corresponds, while the psalm's assertion of fidelity prevents treating the passages as identical explanations of guilt.

relationship: A people sold without a price
rationale: The psalm complains that God sold His people without a price and obtained no abundance in exchange. Isaiah says the people were sold for nothing and will be ransomed without silver. Both use a sale without payment for the people's humiliation; Isaiah also supplies a promise of ransom.

relationship: Reproach and ridicule from neighboring peoples
rationale: Both verses describe becoming a reproach to neighbors and an object of sneering and ridicule to those around. The matching sequence specifies the communal shame beyond a general reference to enemies.

relationship: Becoming a parable among nations
rationale: The community says God made it a parable among nations. Deuteronomy's curses predict becoming a riddle, parable and tale among the nations. The particular description of public disgrace corresponds; the curse's disobedience setting is distinct from Psalm 43's profession of covenant fidelity.

relationship: Shame as a covering
rationale: Psalm 43 says all-day humiliation is before the speaker and the shame of his face covered him. Psalm 68 says embarrassment covered his face alongside endured reproach. Both express disgrace as a covering, while the source's shame of the face covering the speaker is not rewritten as the target's covering of the face.

relationship: Affliction without forgetting divine instruction
rationale: Despite all that happened, the community says it did not forget God or act unjustly toward His covenant. Psalm 118 says sinners' cords entangled the speaker but he did not forget God's law. Both set remembered fidelity against oppression, rather than assuming suffering proves apostasy.

relationship: Humiliation in death's shadow with different stated causes
rationale: Psalm 43 says God humbled the people in affliction and death's shadow covered them. Psalm 106 describes people in death's shadow whose hearts were humbled in toil, then rescued. Psalm 106 expressly attributes their plight to rejected divine counsel; Psalm 43's surrounding profession of fidelity is preserved as a difference.

relationship: Foreign worship as a rejected alternative
rationale: The psalm hypothetically considers forgetting God's name and spreading hands to a foreign god before asserting God's knowledge. Deuteronomy commands service of the Lord and forbids following other gods. The comparison concerns exclusive allegiance; the psalm's conditional words are not turned into an admission of idolatry.

relationship: God searching the hidden heart
rationale: The psalm asks whether God will search out betrayal, because He knows the heart's hidden things. Jeremiah calls the heart deep and declares that the Lord examines hearts and tests kidneys. Both assign knowledge of otherwise concealed inward conduct to divine examination.

relationship: Quotation of sheep destined for slaughter
rationale: Romans explicitly introduces as written the psalm's statement that for God's sake the people are put to death all day and reckoned as sheep for slaughter. Paul uses the quotation amid affliction that cannot separate believers from Christ's love.

relationship: God awakening to act against enemies
rationale: Psalm 43 asks why God sleeps and calls Him to awake and arise. Psalm 77 narrates the Lord awakening like a sleeper and striking enemies backward. Both use waking for renewed divine action, while the lament's appeal is distinct from the other poem's narrative simile.

relationship: Hidden face and apparent divine forgetting
rationale: Psalm 43 asks why God turns His face away and forgets the people's poverty and affliction. Psalm 12 combines the same two complaints, asking how long God will forget the speaker and turn His face away. The parallel keeps the communal and individual objects distinct.

relationship: The soul brought down to the ground
rationale: The community's soul is humbled to dust and its belly clings to earth. Psalm 118 says the speaker's soul clung to the ground and asks for life. Both portray the soul's distress as prostration against the earth, with different accompanying petitions.

relationship: Help and rescue for God's name
rationale: Psalm 43 asks God to arise, help and redeem for His name's sake. Psalm 78 asks God the Savior to help and rescue for the glory of His name, also seeking propitiation for sins. The linked appeal to aid and the divine name is specific, without importing that confession into Psalm 43.

relationship: The heading concerning those who will be changed
rationale: Both headings use the designation 'concerning those who will be changed.' Psalm 44 also names the sons of Korah and a song concerning the beloved, whereas Psalm 68 names David. The connection is the exact unusual heading, without assigning it an unexpressed musical meaning or common occasion.

relationship: Grace associated with lips and spoken words
rationale: The king's lips have grace poured upon them in the psalm. Luke describes hearers marveling at words of grace coming from Jesus' mouth. The correspondence concerns gracious speech; Luke does not explicitly quote this verse or identify the psalm's unnamed king in that scene.

relationship: Royal righteousness and truth
rationale: The psalm commands its royal addressee to prosper and reign for truth, meekness and righteousness. Isaiah describes Jesse's shoot judging the lowly, girded with righteousness and truth. The shared royal qualities are particular, while Isaiah's treatment of the lowly is not rewritten as an identical phrase about meekness.

relationship: The throne and upright scepter quoted concerning the Son
rationale: Hebrews expressly introduces the throne enduring for the age and the scepter of uprightness as words concerning the Son. These correspond to Psalm 44's address to God concerning His enduring throne and upright royal rod.

relationship: Quotation of anointing beyond companions
rationale: Hebrews repeats the love of righteousness, hatred of lawlessness and consequent anointing by God with oil of exultation beyond companions. Its preceding verse identifies this speech as concerning the Son; the extended sequence corresponds directly to the psalm.

relationship: A woman honored at the king's right
rationale: The psalm places the queen at the king's right in golden clothing. Kings describes a throne placed for Solomon's mother Bathsheba, who sits at his right. The court position is comparable, but the psalm's queen is not identified as Bathsheba, and standing is not conflated with sitting.

relationship: Parental ties and a new marital relationship
rationale: The royal poem tells the daughter to forget her people and father's house before describing the king's desire. Genesis says a man leaves father and mother and cleaves to his wife. The departure from parental ties is comparable within these relational settings, with the addressed woman and the departing man kept distinct.

relationship: Foreign gifts and royal homage
rationale: Psalm 44 describes Tyre's daughters bowing to him with gifts and the rich entreating the addressed woman's favor. Psalm 71 describes foreign kings offering gifts and bowing before the king. Both join foreign wealth and royal homage, without merging the different recipients or foreign groups.

relationship: Joyful entrance into royal or divine presence
rationale: The companions are led with gladness and exultation into the king's sanctuary. Psalm 99 commands service to the Lord with gladness and entrance before Him with exultation. The paired expressions and movement into presence correspond, without identifying the psalm's royal procession as the same event.

relationship: An enduring royal name and the response of peoples
rationale: Psalm 44 promises remembrance of the addressee's name through generations and the peoples' enduring thanksgiving. Psalm 71 asks that the king's name remain blessed through the ages and describes all nations calling him blessed. Both connect the royal name's endurance with a response extending beyond one people.

relationship: God as refuge and help in distress
rationale: Psalm 45 calls God refuge, strength and help in afflictions. Psalm 9 says the Lord became refuge for the needy and helper at fitting times in distress. The paired descriptions of refuge and aid in distress ground both statements of reliance.

relationship: Fearlessness grounded in God's presence
rationale: Psalm 45's confession of God as refuge leads to refusal to fear even amid upheaval of earth and mountains. Psalm 22 refuses fear even in death's shadow because God is with the speaker. The danger differs, but both expressly connect fearlessness in extreme peril with divine protection and presence.

relationship: Roaring waters and the voices of rivers
rationale: Psalm 45 depicts waters roaring and disturbed, with mountains disturbed 'at his might.' Psalm 92 gives rivers raised voices and calls the sea's surges and the Lord on high wondrous. The audible waters are the particular poetic correspondence; the comparison does not independently resolve Psalm 45's pronoun.

relationship: A river associated with God's holy dwelling
rationale: Psalm 45 joins a river's streams gladdening God's city with the Most High's sanctified dwelling. Ezekiel sees water flowing from the house by the altar and becoming a river that brings health and life. The holy dwelling and beneficial waters are comparable; the psalm does not identify its river as Ezekiel's vision.

relationship: Divine presence and the unshaken city
rationale: Psalm 45 says God is in the city's midst, she will not be shaken and He will help her. Psalm 124 says the one dwelling in Jerusalem will never be shaken and describes the Lord surrounding His people. Divine presence and protection explain the stated stability in both, with different spatial images.

relationship: The divine voice shaking the earth
rationale: Psalm 45 describes God's voice and the earth being shaken amid disturbed nations and kingdoms. Psalm 28 specifically attributes the shaking of the wilderness to the Lord's voice. Both assign the disturbance of a terrestrial place to divine speech.

relationship: Jacob's God as protector
rationale: The refrain confesses that Jacob's God is the community's supporter. Psalm 19 asks that the name of Jacob's God protect the addressee in affliction. The particular designation and protective role connect assurance and petition.

relationship: Invitation to come and see God's works
rationale: Both verses invite the audience to come and see God's works. Psalm 45 points to wonders on earth, while Psalm 65 describes His counsels concerning humanity as fearsome. The repeated invitation frames divine deeds as grounds for recognition and praise.

relationship: God ending war by breaking weapons
rationale: Psalm 45 describes God ending wars, shattering the bow, breaking a weapon and burning shields. Hosea promises that God will shatter bow, sword and war from the land. Both directly combine divine action against weapons with the cessation of war, without changing shields into chariots.

relationship: War ended through the removal of weapons
rationale: Psalm 45 describes wars ended and weapons broken or burned. Isaiah describes nations beating swords into plows and spears into sickles and ceasing to wage war. Both connect peace with weapons losing their military use, while destruction and conversion into tools remain different actions.

relationship: Ceasing human action before God's power
rationale: Psalm 45 commands the audience to cease activity and know God, following the description of His ending of wars. Moses tells the people to stand and behold divine salvation, for the Lord will fight while they keep silence. Both place human cessation alongside recognition of divine action, without equating the two occasions.

relationship: same-chapter protective refrain
rationale: The closing statement repeats that the Lord of powers is with the people and Jacob's God is their supporter. Its return after the descriptions of God's works and ended warfare reinforces the assurance stated earlier in the poem.

relationship: Clapping and exultation in praise
rationale: Psalm 46 calls all nations to clap their hands and shout to God with exultation. Psalm 97 personifies rivers clapping and mountains exulting before divine judgment. The paired gestures of praise occur with human peoples and natural features as different subjects.

relationship: God as great King beyond one nation
rationale: Psalm 46 calls the Most High a great King over all the earth. Malachi's divine rebuke declares, 'I am a great King,' and says His name is manifest among nations. The shared royal designation has a scope beyond one people, expressed in praise and rebuke respectively.

relationship: Peoples subjected beneath the speaker
rationale: Psalm 46 says God subjected peoples under the community and nations under its feet. Psalm 17 describes God subjecting peoples beneath the individual speaker. The action and spatial expression correspond, while the collective and individual recipients differ.

relationship: Divine choice, love and inheritance
rationale: Psalm 46 says God chose His inheritance for the people, 'the beauty of Jacob, which He loved'. Deuteronomy connects God's love of the fathers with choosing their seed and giving land to inherit. Both join choice, love and an inheritance given to the people, without changing 'His inheritance' into their independent choice.

relationship: Ascent accompanied by shout and trumpet
rationale: The psalm says God ascended with a shout and the Lord with a trumpet's sound. Samuel describes David and Israel bringing up the Lord's ark with shouting and a trumpet's sound. The ceremonial sound and upward movement correspond; this does not prove that the psalm identifies that precise ark procession.

relationship: Music and understanding
rationale: The psalm commands music with understanding because God is King of all the earth. Paul says he will sing with the spirit and also with the mind. Both expressly join song with intellectual participation, while Paul's surrounding argument specifically concerns intelligibility in the Church.

relationship: Divine kingship over the nations
rationale: Psalm 46 says God reigned over nations and sits on His holy throne. Psalm 21 explains that kingship belongs to the Lord and He is master of the nations. Both explicitly connect divine kingship with authority over nations, not merely one earthly realm.

relationship: Weekday designations in Psalm headings
rationale: Psalm 47's heading specifies the second day of the week, while Psalm 23's specifies the first. The exact weekday notices form a concrete heading comparison; neither a shared author nor an unexpressed performance occasion is inferred.

relationship: The repeated acclamation of the Lord's greatness
rationale: Psalm 47 declares the Lord great and greatly to be praised in His city and holy mountain. Psalm 95 uses the same acclamation before calling Him fearsome above all gods. The repeated praise formula occurs with different following descriptions.

relationship: Jerusalem as the city of the great King
rationale: The psalm calls Zion the city of the great King. Jesus forbids swearing by Jerusalem because it is the city of the great King. The distinctive city designation supplies the connection; the Gospel applies it within teaching about oaths.

relationship: God's presence supporting the city
rationale: Psalm 47 says God is known in her citadels when He supports her. Psalm 45 says God is in the city's midst, preventing its shaking and bringing help. Both connect the city's security with divine presence and support, while keeping citadels and the city as distinct expressions.

relationship: Terror compared to childbirth
rationale: The psalm describes trembling and pains like those of a woman giving birth. Jeremiah's people report paralyzed hands and affliction seizing them like childbirth pains after hearing of an approaching force. The same bodily comparison expresses fear, without equating the unnamed kings with Jeremiah's people.

relationship: A destructive wind and ships at sea
rationale: Psalm 47 says God will shatter Tarshish ships with a violent wind. Ezekiel's address to the trading city describes the south wind shattering her in the sea after her rowers led her out. Wind-driven maritime destruction is comparable, but the wind, subject and occasion are not harmonized.

relationship: God founding Zion
rationale: Psalm 47 says God founded His city forever after describing what was heard and seen there. Psalm 86 names Mother Zion and says the Most High Himself founded her. Both expressly attribute the city's foundation to God, while Psalm 86's verse does not repeat the temporal qualification.

relationship: God's name honored across the earth
rationale: Psalm 47 extends God's praise, like His name, to the earth's limits. Malachi says His name has been glorified among nations from sunrise to sunset, with incense and pure sacrifice in every place. Both give the honor of God's name a worldwide scope, with different forms of worship specified.

relationship: Zion and Judea's daughters rejoicing at judgments
rationale: Both verses join Zion's rejoicing with the daughters of Judea exulting because of God's judgments. Psalm 47 voices the desired response and Psalm 96 describes it as heard and enacted; the distinctive combination is shared.

relationship: Telling the next generation
rationale: After commands concerning the city's strength and citadels, Psalm 47 gives the purpose of telling another generation. Psalm 77 repeatedly directs the transmission of God's deeds and instruction to children and the generation to come. The shared purpose is deliberate intergenerational testimony, with different material being described.

relationship: God shepherding His people
rationale: Psalm 47 identifies the community's God forever and says He will shepherd them through the ages. Psalm 22 confesses that the Lord shepherds the individual speaker. Both assign shepherding to God; the communal duration is not rewritten as shepherding only until death.

relationship: Rich and poor considered together
rationale: Psalm 48 explicitly includes rich and poor together in its audience for teaching on wealth and mortality. Proverbs brings rich and poor together and says the Lord made both. The paired economic groups are jointly placed under a condition beyond their wealth, with mortality and common creation remaining different emphases.

relationship: Parables and riddles as modes of instruction
rationale: Psalm 48 says the speaker will incline his ear to a parable and open a riddle with a psaltery. Psalm 77 says he will open his mouth in parables and utter riddles from the beginning. The two named forms of enigmatic instruction correspond, without making listening and speaking the same action.

relationship: Confidence in strength and wealth
rationale: The psalm identifies those trusting their strength and boasting in abundant wealth. Jeremiah forbids the strong from boasting in strength and the rich from boasting in wealth. Both pair these particular grounds of human confidence in a critical setting.

relationship: Wealth as an uncertain ground of confidence
rationale: Psalm 48 introduces people boasting in wealth before discussing redemption prices and the passing of possessions. Timothy is told to forbid the rich from arrogance and hope in uncertain wealth, directing hope to God. The connection concerns misplaced confidence, not a claim that every wealthy person has the same conduct.

relationship: Questions of redemption and life's exchange price
rationale: Psalm 48 says a brother does not redeem, asks whether a person will redeem and says he will not give God his atonement price, continuing with the soul's redemption price in the next unit. Jesus asks what gain of the world benefits someone who forfeits life and what a person can give in exchange for life. Both question material means of securing life without resolving Psalm 48:10's difficult syntax.

relationship: Wise and foolish dying while wealth passes to others
rationale: Psalm 48 says foolish and senseless people perish and leave wealth to strangers after mentioning the wise dying. Ecclesiastes asks how the wise dies with the fool and laments leaving toil to a successor whose wisdom is unknown. Both join common mortality with loss of control over accumulated goods.

relationship: The grave or Hades described as a house
rationale: Psalm 48 calls tombs the enduring houses of those who invoked their names upon their lands. Job conditionally describes Hades as his house and gloom as his bedding. Both use domestic lodging for death's dwelling, while Job's personal lament is distinct from the psalm's observation about the wealthy.

relationship: Human beings compared with beasts
rationale: The psalm says the honored human who did not understand became like senseless beasts. Ecclesiastes compares humans and beasts through their shared death, breath and return to dust. The comparison is explicit in both, but the psalm emphasizes failed understanding rather than merely creaturely mortality.

relationship: Contrasting shepherds in the presence of death
rationale: Psalm 48 pictures people as sheep placed in Hades with death shepherding them. Psalm 22 names the Lord as shepherd and refuses fear while walking in death's shadow because He is present. The shepherd imagery and death setting create a precise contrast between the guides; no identical afterlife account is imposed.

relationship: Hope that God will not leave the soul to Hades
rationale: Psalm 48 expects God to redeem the soul from Hades' hand when He receives the speaker. Psalm 15 says God will not abandon the speaker's soul to Hades. Both contrast Hades with God's saving action for the soul, with redemption and non-abandonment expressed differently.

relationship: Divine rescue from Hades' hand
rationale: The psalm anticipates God redeeming the soul from Hades' hand. Hosea gives God's promise to rescue people from Hades' hand and redeem them from death. The unusual combination of redemption and Hades' hand corresponds, with the individual and plural recipients kept distinct.

relationship: Limits on carrying possessions beyond life
rationale: Psalm 48 says the dying person will not take everything and his glory will not descend with him. Timothy states that people brought nothing into the world and cannot carry anything out. Both limit the retention of possessions beyond life; the psalm's 'not everything' is not silently changed into the letter's 'anything.'

relationship: Death pictured as enduring darkness
rationale: Psalm 48 says the person will enter the generation of his fathers and never see light. Job anticipates going without return to a land of everlasting darkness with no brightness. Both portray departure into death as a lasting loss of light, without identifying the individual experiences.

relationship: same-chapter refrain of uncomprehending human honor
rationale: The final verse repeats the statement that the honored human failed to understand and became like senseless beasts. Its repetition after the discussion of wealth and death closes the warning with the same judgment voiced earlier.

relationship: The span from sunrise to sunset
rationale: Psalm 49 says God spoke and called the earth from the sun's risings to its settings. Psalm 112 uses the same span to command praise of the Lord's name. The geographic or daily formula is shared, with divine summons and human praise remaining different actions.

relationship: Fire before God
rationale: Psalm 49 describes fire burning before the coming God and a great tempest around Him. Psalm 96 describes fire going ahead before Him and setting enemies aflame. Both place fire before God in divine manifestation; the enemy-burning object belongs expressly to Psalm 96.

relationship: Heaven and earth summoned for testimony concerning the people
rationale: Psalm 49 calls heaven above and earth to the judging of God's people. Moses gathers the people's officers and calls heaven and earth as witnesses concerning them. The cosmic summons has a judicial setting in both, with God and Moses as different speakers.

relationship: Covenant established over sacrifices
rationale: Psalm 49 calls for God's holy ones who establish His covenant over sacrifices to be gathered. Exodus narrates burnt offerings and calves, the reading of the covenant book, and covenant blood sprinkled on the people. It supplies a concrete covenant-and-sacrifice comparison without claiming the psalm's gathering is the same ceremony.

relationship: Heavens declaring God's righteousness
rationale: Psalm 49 says the heavens will announce His righteousness because God is judge. Psalm 96 says the heavens announced His righteousness and all peoples saw His glory. The distinctive heavenly proclamation is shared, with future and completed forms preserved.

relationship: God's covenant self-identification to Israel
rationale: God addresses Israel with 'I am God, your God' while testifying to it. The commandments open with the Lord identifying Himself as Israel's God who brought it from Egypt. The repeated self-identification frames divine address to the same covenant people without adding the exodus clause to the psalm.

relationship: Divine knowledge and oversight of birds
rationale: God says He knows all heaven's birds in the psalm. Jesus says no sparrow falls to the ground apart from the Father. Both explicitly extend divine attention to birds, with the psalm asserting knowledge and the Gospel specifying their falling under the Father's oversight.

relationship: The world and its fullness belong to God
rationale: Psalm 49 explains that God would not tell humans if hungry because the inhabited world and its fullness are His. Psalm 23 declares that the earth, its fullness, the inhabited world and its inhabitants belong to the Lord. The ownership statement is the particular basis shared by the two passages.

relationship: God is not sustained by human offerings
rationale: The psalm rhetorically asks whether God will eat bulls' flesh or drink goats' blood. Paul says God is not served by human hands as though needing anything, since He supplies life and everything. Both reject treating divine life as dependent on human provision, with sacrificial food specified only in the psalm.

relationship: A sacrifice of praise
rationale: The psalm commands a praising sacrifice to God as well as repayment of vows. Hebrews calls for a continual sacrifice of praise to God and explains it as lips confessing His name. The praise offering corresponds directly; Hebrews's verse does not restate the vow command.

relationship: Calling in distress, rescue and grateful acknowledgment
rationale: God invites a call in affliction, promises rescue and says the rescued person will glorify Him. Psalm 106 recounts people crying in affliction and being rescued, then calls them to acknowledge God's mercies and wonders. The sequence links appeal, divine rescue and the human response of praise.

relationship: Religious instruction contradicted by conduct
rationale: God asks a sinner why he recites divine decrees and carries the covenant in his mouth; the following rebuke includes running with a thief and sharing a portion with adulterers. Romans asks whether one who teaches against theft and adultery practices them. Both challenge a mismatch between professed instruction and conduct, with association and the questioned acts expressed differently.

relationship: Casting God's words behind the body
rationale: The psalm accuses the sinner of hating instruction and casting God's words behind him. The prayer recorded in Nehemiah says the people cast God's law behind their bodies while withdrawing from Him. The unusual bodily image expresses deliberate rejection of divine instruction in both.

relationship: Joining those who steal
rationale: The psalm rebukes someone who runs with a thief and also has a portion with adulterers. Proverbs depicts people inviting the son to join in seizing property and sharing a common purse, then forbids walking with them. The concrete comparison is participation with thieves; the adultery clause is not transferred into Proverbs's scene.

relationship: Evil and deceitful speech
rationale: Psalm 49 accuses the mouth of multiplying wickedness and the tongue of weaving deceit. Psalm 33 commands restraint of the tongue from evil and lips from deceit. The paired evils and organs of speech correspond in accusation and admonition.

relationship: Hostility involving brothers and a mother's sons
rationale: Psalm 49 describes speech against one's brother and a stumbling block against one's mother's son. Psalm 68 describes the speaker estranged from brothers and a foreigner to his mother's sons. Both use the paired kinship expressions for fractured family relations, without equating slander with estrangement or identifying the speakers.

relationship: Divine forbearance followed by exposure of wrongdoing
rationale: Psalm 49 says God's silence was mistaken for likeness to the sinner, before He promises rebuke and exposure. Isaiah says God sees and overlooks the addressee, who did not fear Him, then promises to proclaim His righteousness and the person's evils. Both join withheld immediate response with disregard and coming disclosure, using different descriptions of that response.

relationship: No rescuer from divine seizure
rationale: The psalm warns those forgetting God to understand lest He seize them with no one to rescue. Deuteronomy declares God's power to kill, make alive, wound and heal, and that no one can deliver from His hands. The threat's lack of an alternative deliverer is explicit in both.

relationship: same-chapter return to the praising sacrifice
rationale: The closing verse says a praising sacrifice glorifies God and connects the way with divine salvation. It returns to the command to offer a praising sacrifice in verse 14, enclosing the intervening rebuke with the poem's positive account of worship.

relationship: Nathan's visit named in the Psalm heading
rationale: The heading places the psalm when Nathan the prophet came to David after the Bathsheba encounter. Samuel specifically narrates the Lord sending Nathan to David and Nathan coming in to him. The shared named visit is grounded in the surrounding narrative of David's wrongdoing.

relationship: The Bathsheba encounter named in the heading
rationale: The heading explicitly situates Nathan's visit after David went in to Bathsheba. Samuel identifies Bathsheba as Uriah's wife and narrates David taking her and lying with her. The comparison follows the heading's named event rather than a general association with David.

relationship: God wiping out lawless acts
rationale: Psalm 50 appeals to divine mercy and compassion for the blotting out of the speaker's lawless deed. Isaiah presents God as the One who wipes out lawless acts and will not remember. The erasure of wrongdoing corresponds as requested mercy and divine declaration.

relationship: Washing and cleansing from evil
rationale: The psalm asks God to wash the speaker from lawlessness and cleanse him from sin. Isaiah commands people to wash themselves, become clean and remove evils. Both use washing and cleansing for moral evil, while the petition to God and command to the people have different immediate agents.

relationship: Quotation about God justified in His words
rationale: Romans explicitly cites the psalm's statement that God may be justified in His words and prevail when He is judged. Paul uses it to uphold God's truth despite human unfaithfulness. Both retain God as the one described as being judged, rather than silently reversing that wording.

relationship: Impurity associated with life's beginning
rationale: The psalmist speaks of being conceived in lawless deeds and sins. Job asks who can be clean from filth and answers no one, even if life is one day. Both place impurity at the outset of human life; neither comparison specifies an unnamed act by the psalmist's mother or settles a theory of inherited guilt.

relationship: Hidden divine wisdom made known
rationale: The psalm says God revealed unseen and hidden things of His wisdom to the speaker. Paul describes God's hidden wisdom and says God revealed the prepared things through the Spirit. Concealed wisdom becomes known by divine disclosure in both; the psalm is not said to name Paul's particular proclamation.

relationship: Hyssop and sprinkling for cleansing
rationale: Psalm 50 anticipates sprinkling with hyssop and becoming clean. Leviticus includes hyssop in the cleansing rite and commands sprinkling the person seven times. The distinctive material and cleansing action correspond, without asserting that the penitent's sin is a diagnosis of leprosy.

relationship: Sins cleansed to snow's whiteness
rationale: The psalm anticipates washing and becoming whiter than snow. Isaiah promises to whiten purple-red sins like snow and scarlet sins like wool. Both use snow's whiteness for removal of moral stain, while the psalm's comparative 'whiter' differs from Isaiah's simile.

relationship: Joy and bones expressing praise
rationale: Psalm 50 anticipates hearing exultation and gladness, and humbled bones will exult. Psalm 34 anticipates the soul's exultation and all the bones asking who is like the rescuing Lord. Both give the bones a voice or action within joyful praise, with distinct statements about what the bones do.

relationship: All sins moved out of view
rationale: The psalm asks God to turn His face away from sins and blot out all lawless acts. Isaiah's prayer says God cast all the speaker's sins behind him. Both express removal of all wrongdoing through spatial or erasure language; Isaiah's actual 'behind me' is not changed to 'behind God.'

relationship: Cleansing, a new heart and renewed spirit
rationale: The psalm asks God to create a clean heart and renew an upright spirit within the speaker. Ezekiel promises cleansing, a new heart and new spirit, and also God's own Spirit placed within the people. Both locate inward renewal in divine action, while the psalm's upright spirit is not simply equated with every spirit expression in Ezekiel.

relationship: The feared removal of God's Spirit
rationale: Psalm 50 asks God not to remove His holy Spirit from the speaker. Samuel describes the Lord's Spirit departing from Saul. The narrative gives a specific contrast to the prayer against removal; it does not identify Saul as this psalm's speaker.

relationship: Joy in divine salvation
rationale: Psalm 50 asks restoration of the exultation of God's salvation. Psalm 12 anticipates the heart exulting in God's salvation after hope in mercy. The particular joy is tied to salvation in both; the request for restoration and the anticipated response remain distinct.

relationship: Teaching God's way to those needing correction
rationale: Psalm 50 anticipates teaching God's ways to the lawless so the ungodly turn back to Him. Psalm 24 says the Lord gives sinners instruction in the way and teaches the meek His ways. Both connect divine ways and instruction directed toward those needing guidance, with the penitent and God as different teachers.

relationship: Bloodshed in the Nathan and David context
rationale: Psalm 50 asks rescue from bloodshed, and its heading names Nathan's visit after Bathsheba. In that visit Nathan specifically accuses David of killing Uriah through the sons of Ammon. The narrative supplies concrete bloodshed within the named context; the psalm's request itself does not name Uriah or specify the exact sense of deliverance.

relationship: God opening the mouth for speech
rationale: The psalm says God will open the speaker's lips and the mouth will announce His praise. God tells Ezekiel He will open his mouth so that he speaks a divine message. Both place the opening of speech organs under divine agency, while praise and prophetic address remain distinct utterances.

relationship: Sacrifices and burnt offerings not desired
rationale: Psalm 50 says a desired sacrifice would have been given, but God will not delight in burnt offerings. Psalm 39 says God did not desire sacrifice and offering or request burnt and sin offerings. The explicit negative statements concerning these offerings correspond; Psalm 50's later restored offerings are still read in context.

relationship: Ritual offering measured against another response to God
rationale: The psalm denies divine delight in burnt offerings before identifying a broken spirit and humbled heart as sacrifice. Samuel asks whether burnt offerings and sacrifices are as desirable as listening, and values obedience above sacrifice. Both refuse to treat ritual offerings as sufficient, while humility and obedience are distinct positive responses.

relationship: God's favorable regard for the brokenhearted
rationale: Psalm 50 calls a broken spirit God's sacrifice and says He will not despise a broken and humbled heart. Isaiah describes the Most High giving patience to the fainthearted and life to the brokenhearted. Both affirm divine regard for brokenhearted people, without changing Isaiah's resting among holy ones into a different dwelling claim.

relationship: Jerusalem's wall and God's favorable action
rationale: The psalm asks God to do good to Zion and asks that Jerusalem's walls be built. Nehemiah calls for rebuilding Jerusalem's wall and reports God's good hand upon him. The particular city, wall-building and favorable divine action correspond, without assigning the psalm's request to Nehemiah's historical occasion.

relationship: A sacrifice of righteousness
rationale: Psalm 50 anticipates God's delight in a sacrifice of righteousness after the prayer for Zion and Jerusalem. Psalm 4 commands offering a sacrifice of righteousness and hoping in the Lord. The specific description of acceptable sacrifice connects the passages and qualifies any reading of Psalm 50 as rejecting every offering without distinction.
